name: Ammiel
title: Spy from the tribe of Dan who explored Canaan
summary: As the representative for the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli was chosen to take part in the fateful spying mission when Moses sent twelve men from the wilderness of Paran to scout out the land of Canaan. Through forty days of reconnaissance—from the wilderness of Zin in the south to Rehob near Lebo-Hamath in the north—the spies gained a complete picture of both the richness and the challenges of the promised land. Despite the land’s fertility and abundance, Ammiel was overwhelmed by fear of Canaan’s powerful inhabitants and fortified cities. Along with nine other spies, he spread discouragement throughout all Israel’s assembly by claiming that the people there were too strong to overcome. This report triggered a serious crisis of faith that erupted into open rebellion against Moses and Aaron, with the people even wanting to return to Egypt. God’s judgment on the ten unfaithful spies was immediate and final: they died from a plague before the Lord. Only Joshua and Caleb, who had held fast to their faith in God’s power and promises, were spared and eventually allowed to enter the promised land. Ammiel’s story is a powerful reminder of how fear and unbelief can undermine God’s people in their calling and hinder the fulfillment of His promises.

keyEvents.title: Selected as a Scout for the Tribe of Dan
keyEvents.description: Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was chosen as the representative from the tribe of Dan to be one of the twelve scouts sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan.

keyEvents.title: Sent Out to Scout the Land of Canaan
keyEvents.description: Moses sent Ammiel and the other eleven scouts from the wilderness of Paran to investigate the land, its people, cities, and resources.

keyEvents.title: Exploring the Promised Land
keyEvents.description: The scouts, including Ammiel, spent forty days exploring the land of Canaan from the wilderness of Zin in the south to Rehob near Lebo-Hamath in the north.

keyEvents.title: The Negative Report
keyEvents.description: Ammiel was among the ten scouts who gave a negative report about the land, claiming that its people were too strong to be defeated, which caused fear and discouragement among the Israelites.

keyEvents.title: The People's Rebellion
keyEvents.description: The negative report from Ammiel and the other scouts led the entire congregation to grumble against Moses and Aaron and wish to return to Egypt.

keyEvents.title: God's Judgment on the Unfaithful Scouts
keyEvents.description: Ammiel and the other nine scouts who had spread fear among the people were struck down by a plague and died before the Lord as punishment for their unbelief.

versions.summary: Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was one of the twelve spies that Moses sent out to explore the land of Canaan. He represented the tribe of Dan. He was among the ten spies who returned with a negative report and discouraged the people from entering the promised land.
versions.title: The Spy from the Tribe of Dan
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Scout from the Tribe of Dan' is functional but could be made more descriptive by including context about the scouting mission to Canaan.; [major] Ammiel is not described as a 'warrior' in the Bible. His primary role was that of a scout or envoy. He was a tribal chief or representative for Dan, but the role of 'warrior' is not documented. 'Leader' can be retained as tribal representative, but 'scout' should be added as his main role.; [minor] The description mentions 'the other eleven scouts' – this is correct (12 total minus Ammiel = 11 others), but it would be a small stylistic improvement to clarify this.; [minor] It states 'from the Wilderness of Sin to Rehob' – the correct phrasing is 'from the Wilderness of Sin to Rehob near Lebo-Hamat' (Num 13:21). The Wilderness of Sin and the Wilderness of Sinai are different locations.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile should include footnotes covering linguistic, historical, or theological aspects, such as the meaning of the name, the scouting mission in context, or the fate of the ten scouts.

versions.summary:
Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was one of the twelve spies whom Moses sent out to explore the land of Canaan.  
He represented the tribe of Dan in this important mission.  
After forty days of reconnaissance, Ammiel was among the ten spies who returned with a negative report and claimed that the inhabitants of Canaan were too powerful to be overcome.  
This treacherous report spread fear among the Israelites and led to the people’s rebellion against Moses and Aaron.  
As punishment for spreading doubt and discouragement, Ammiel and the nine other unfaithful spies were struck by plague and died in the Lord’s presence.  
Only Joshua and Caleb, who held fast to their trust in God, were spared.
versions.title: Spy from the tribe of Dan who explored Canaan
versions.reason: [major] Ammiel lived during the time of the wilderness wanderings, before the conquest of Canaan began. The spying mission took place while the Israelites were still in the wilderness. The correct era should be 'exodus' (the wilderness wanderings), not 'conquest', since the conquest only began after the wilderness period ended and under Joshua's leadership.; [minor] The lifespan 'c. 1400 BC' is somewhat imprecise. The spying mission is traditionally dated to c. 1444–1400 BC depending on the chronological framework. A phrasing such as 'c. 1400s BC' could be more comprehensive.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but it could be strengthened with a brief theological reflection on what Ammiel's action represents in a broader salvation-historical perspective – the lack of faith as a contrast to Joshua and Caleb's faith.; [minor] In the event 'Sent out to spy out Canaan', it describes 'eleven other spies', which is actually correct (eleven others, totaling twelve including Ammiel). No error, but a confirmation.

versions.summary: Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was a representative from the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies that Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran to explore the land of Canaan. After forty days of reconnaissance throughout the land, from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob near Lebo-Hamath, Ammiel was among the ten spies who returned with a discouraging and fear-filled report. Despite the land being rich and fertile, these spies claimed that the inhabitants of Canaan were too powerful and their cities too fortified for Israel to overcome them. This lack of trust in God's promise to give them the land sowed fear throughout the congregation and triggered a rebellion against Moses and Aaron. As a consequence of having undermined the people's faith and spread discouragement, Ammiel and the nine other unfaithful spies were struck by God's judgment and died from a plague before the Lord. Only Joshua and Caleb, who held fast to their trust in God's promises, were spared and eventually allowed to enter the promised land. Ammiel's fate serves as a warning about the consequences of unbelief when facing God's promises.
versions.title: Spy from the tribe of Dan who explored Canaan
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good and detailed, but since there have already been two versions with a similar opening ('Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was one of the twelve spies...'), the text should be rephrased to avoid similarity with earlier versions. A new angle could provide better variation.; [minor] The description mentions 'the Wilderness of Zin' as the starting point for the exploration. In Numbers 13:21, it is indeed the Wilderness of Zin (Negev/Wilderness of Zin) that is mentioned, but the actual starting point for the spies was the Wilderness of Paran (Numbers 13:3). The Wilderness of Zin (Hebrew: מִדְבַּר־צִן) is the place they explored from the south. The wording could be misunderstood.; [minor] The word 'entre' (in 'finally entered the promised land') is a Norwegianization of the French 'entrer'. A more natural Norwegian expression would be 'go into' or 'take possession of'.; [minor] Same issue with the word 'unfaithfulness' – it works, but the context suggests that 'unbelief' alone is sufficient and more precise here, since 'unfaithfulness' often connotes breaking a promise to a person rather than lacking trust in God.

footnotes.text: The name Ammiel (Hebrew: עַמִּיאֵל, 'Ammi'el) means 'my people are God' or 'God is one of my kin'. The name is composed of 'am' (people) and 'El' (God), expressing a theological confession about God's belonging to and closeness with His people.

The spying mission in Numbers 13 was a decisive turning point in the wilderness journey. The twelve spies each represented one tribe, giving the report an official and representative character as a national reconnaissance. That ten out of twelve spies gave a negative report illustrates the depth of the people's crisis of trust in God's promises.

The punishment on the ten spies—that they died by plague before the Lord (Num 14:37)—underscores the seriousness of spreading fear and doubt among God's people. In biblical theology, this is presented as a paradigmatic example of unbelief with fatal consequences. Only Joshua and Caleb survived out of the twelve, and were finally allowed to enter the promised land.

The tribe of Dan, which Ammiel represented, was later assigned an area in the southwestern part of Canaan but had great difficulties taking possession of it and eventually migrated northward (Judg 18). There is a remarkable connection between Ammiel's negative report about the inhabitants of the land and the tribe of Dan's later problems with occupying their allotted territory.

There are several people named Ammiel in the Old Testament, including the father of Bathsheba (1 Chr 3:5) and the father of Makir from Lo-debar (2 Sam 9:4–5). The name's popularity testifies that the theological confession it expresses—'my people are God'—was important in Israelite naming tradition.

Archaeological research on city walls in Canaan from the Late Bronze Age confirms that several cities in the region had massive fortifications, which may explain the spies' fear. Excavations in cities such as Hazor, Lachish, and Megiddo show that these cities were well fortified with thick walls and gate complexes.
